artworks.title: Bessie Smith Close Up
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
Born into poverty in Chattanooga, Tennessee, Bessie Smith (1894–1937) defied the circumstances of her upbringing to become the most celebrated blues artist of her time. Known as the “Empress of the Blues,” she began her career traveling through the South singing in tent shows, bars, and theaters before making her way to Philadelphia, which she would eventually call home.
By the early 1920s, Smith recorded more than 160 songs for Columbia Records, becoming the first blues singer to reach mass audiences and the highest-paid Black entertainer of her time. Her lyrics were powerful narratives of the African American experience, focusing on social and economic struggles, racial injustice, gender inequality, and the complexities of love. Stella Bloch painted Smith during this career high, capturing her prideful posture as she projected her voice to fill large theaters.
Smith’s life was cut short in 1937 at age 43 following a car accident near Clarksdale, Mississippi, where racial segregation at Southern hospitals delayed necessary medical care, and her injuries became fatal. Despite this tragedy, her legacy endures. With her barrier-breaking career, Smith forged a path for generations of Black artists to follow. She was posthumously inducted into the inaugural class of the Blues Hall of Fame (1980) and into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame (1989).
Staff Favorites from the Mattatuck Collection
January 18, 2026 – April 12, 2026
“I love Bessie Smith. I remember going to see her with my mother and grandmother in the city. She was such an exceptional jazz singer. She would always be wearing a beautiful rose in her hair. Her expression comes off as very sad to me in this work.” - Staff Member: Barbara
Hepburn, Visitor Services
The Art of Leisure
April 12, 2025 – June 15, 2025
Bessie Smith, known as the “Empress of Blues,” received acclaim for her powerful and emotive voice as well as her captivating stage presence. Artist and dancer Stella Bloch, a longtime admirer of Smith, captures the famed singer in a reverent moment of song. Bloch’s expressive brush strokes seem melodic themselves, alternating between short and long beats on the paper.

artworks.title: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
Charlotte Perkins Gilman (1860–1935), born in Hartford, was a feminist, writer, and advocate for social reform, promoting the professionalization of domestic responsibilities and childcare, among other strategies toward gender equality and economic independence for women. Her 1892 short story “The Yellow Wall-Paper” describes one woman’s experience with a “rest cure” for “temporary nervous depression” (likely what we understand today to be postpartum depression). In the story, the protagonist’s physician-husband forces her to remain in a summer home with no intellectual stimulation; she descends into madness, a clear statement on the negative psychological and emotional impact of restricting women’s ambitions outside the domestic space.
Depicted here by contemporary artist Suzanne Benton, Gilman remains an inspiring writer and thinker to many feminists, writers, sociologists, and scholars today.

artworks.title: Dede Pierce on Trumpet, Presentation Hall, New Orleans, 1972
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
Joseph “De De” De Lacroix Pierce (1904–1973), born into a musical Afro-French Creole family, established himself in the 1920s as a talented trumpeter and vocalist popular in New Orleans’s vibrant brass band scene.
In 1933, he met pianist and vocalist Billie Pierce, whom he married, marking the beginning of their legacy as a musical duo. They became a regular house band at the Luthjens Dance Hall and recorded numerous jazz and ragtime albums together.
Despite health setbacks in the 1950s—Dede lost his eyesight from glaucoma and Billie suffered a stroke—the couple returned to recording and performing by the end of that decade and through the rest of their lives. Widely acclaimed, they performed at the now-legendary jazz venue Preservation Hall in the French Quarter of New Orleans. The last decade of the Pierces’ lives—including the year depicted in this portrait—was spent recording, touring, and playing to adoring audiences.

artworks.title: Two Ladies
artworks.description:
Included in the exhibitions:
Between Worlds: Stories of Artists and Migration, September 24, 2023 – January 7, 2024
Two Ladies creates a stark contrast between the promise and reality of America. Carlos Hernández Chávez emigrated from Mexico to the United States as a young adult, following love and an audition with the rock band, The Animals. While he has thrived in this country, Hernández Chávez sees the struggles many people face. He created Two Ladies by collaging photographs he took in New York City. In 1986, the year he made this print, The Statue of Liberty celebrated its 100th birthday. In this image, we see Lady Liberty from the back, through barbed wire, while the homeless woman’s body obscures the year on the poster behind her, suggesting that the liberty the Statue represents has yet to be achieved.
La Onda Chicana, March 5, 2023 – June 1, 2023
Created by collaging photographs he took on trips to New York City and imbued with a vibrant palette, Two Ladies creates a stark contrast between the promise and reality of America. “The title came from the common reference to the statue as ‘Lady Liberty’ and the pejorative ‘bag lady’ that many people use to refer to homeless women. It’s sort of ironic that the homeless woman was sleeping right at the boarding station to Liberty Island,” says Chávez. Furthermore, 1986 was the 100-year anniversary of The Statue of Liberty. Here we see her from behind while the body of the homeless woman obscures the year on the poster behind her, suggesting that the liberty the statue represents has yet to be achieved.
Creada mediante fotografías combinadas que tomó en viajes a la ciudad de Nueva York e imbuida de una paleta vibrante, Two Ladies crea un marcado contraste entre la promesa y la realidad de Estados Unidos. “El título proviene de la referencia común a la estatua como ‘Lady Liberty’ y la peyorativa ‘señora de la bolsa’ que muchas personas usan para referirse a las mujeres sin hogar. Es un poco irónico que la mujer sin hogar estuviera durmiendo justo en la estación de embarque a Liberty Island,” dice Chávez. Además, 1986 fue el 100 aniversario de la Estatua de la Libertad. Aquí la vemos desde atrás mientras el cuerpo de la mujer sin hogar oscurece el año en el cartel detrás de ella, lo que sugiere que la libertad que representa la estatua aún no se ha logrado.

artworks.title: Karen Booth
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
George Deem is best known for reworking classic images from art history with contemporary spins. He grew up working alongside his father at his cantaloupe farm and enrolled at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, though he was drafted into the army just a year later, in 1953. Stationed in the historic German town of Heidelberg, he visited cities including Florence, Venice, Paris, and London, seeing artistic masterworks. Upon his return to the United States, he finished his degree at the Art Institute, then moved to New York City where he worked at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and developed his unique painting style.
This portrait differs from Deem’s typical fragmenting and reworking of iconic images. He had known a Karen “Kathy” Booth as a dancer and admired her artistry, creating portraits of her at four angles while making a full turn. Presented here is her final angle, with the dancer’s gaze directed upward in a bold finish, offering a portrait of both a dancer and her dance.

artworks.title: Portrait of Hope Elizabeth Robinson (Phipard)
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
In 1902, artist N.C. Wyeth attended the Howard Pyle School of Illustration Art in Wilmington, Delaware, and soon went on to become one of the United States’ most well-known illustrators, completing more than a thousand book and magazine illustrations and more than 3,000 paintings.
Despite his commercial success, Wyeth was frustrated by his inability to escape the demands and limitations of illustration. He painted still lifes and portraits, which he loved, whenever he could. This painting is a prime example of Wyeth’s skill for portraiture. While living in Needham, Massachusetts, he captured Hope Elizabeth Robinson (1914–unknown), the daughter of Edward Kilburn Robinson, an editor at publishing company Ginn & Company, and Hope Dunlap Robinson, an illustrator of children’s books. Wyeth and the Robinsons had been family friends, perhaps connected through their publishing circles.

artworks.title: 'topher (Ruminations)
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
Born in rural east Texas, Robert Rauschenberg became a groundbreaking artist who worked across mediums and played a role in shaping multiple postwar American art movements.
He began his Ruminations series when he was in his mid-70s, the year after a major career retrospective at the Guggenheim Museum in New York City—perhaps a time of reflection for the artist. The series provides an intimate lens into the artist’s life. ‘topher presents a disjointed family portrait of Rauschenberg; his ex-wife, the artist Susan Weil; and their son, Christopher. Rauschenberg and Weil were married for less than a year and during that time they collaborated and explored different methods of photographic production together, remaining integral to each other’s lives even after marriage.
The photograph of Weil takes up most of the print, offering a central base for the smaller vignettes of Rauschenberg and his son. The separation of Rauschenberg’s own image perhaps suggests his feelings of distance following his divorce. In a 2016 oral history, Christopher reflected fondly on his relationship with his father, but described a particular closeness with his mother, living together when he was a child in a happy “two-person household.”
Ruminations: Rauschenberg at 100
September 25, 2025 – December 7, 2025
‘topher presents a disjointed family portrait of Rauschenberg, his ex-wife Susan Weil (American, b. 1930), and their son Christopher. Rauschenberg and Weil were students together, first in Paris and then at the avante garde Black Mountain College in North Carolina. During their brief romantic relationship, they collaborated and explored different methods of photographic production in their art. Although the pair were married for less than a year, they remained integral to each other’s lives.
The photograph of Susan takes up most of the print and provides a grounded base for the smaller vignettes of Bob and Christopher. While her image supports that of Christopher, Rauschenberg’s photograph is separated from the pair in a shot that feels more posed than the others. The composition might suggest Rauschenberg’s feelings of distance following his divorce from Weir. While Christopher reflected fondly on his relationship with his father, he described living with his mother in a happy “two-person household.” [BLP, Ruminations: Rauschenberg at 100, 2025]

artworks.title: Portrait of Jane Peterson
artworks.medium: Watercolor, paper mounted on canvas, painting
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
Elsie Whitmore Southwick Clark’s portrait of Jane Peterson (1876–1965) captures the globe-trotting artist in a rare moment of stillness. Dressed in her walking clothes and carrying her portable supplies box, Peterson is depicted ready to explore and paint new lands.
Born in Illinois, Jane Peterson would become one of the foremost women painters in New York by 1925. Her story is one of a woman with an unshakable purpose, an independent mind, and a keen interest in art and painting. She often told the story that despite her family’s poor background, in 1895, her mother sent her to study art at Pratt Institute in New York with $300 to cover travel expenses, tuition, and initial living expenses.
At a time when society expected women to dedicate their lives to domesticity and household management, Peterson’s career challenged social norms. She found international success as she traveled across the United States—especially the Southwest and New England—Europe, and Africa. Peterson met Clark in 1908 while they were both in Paris; they had built a friendship for several years before this portrait was painted. They both grew in their careers, sometimes participating in the same exhibitions, galleries, and artists’ clubs, and holding prominent places in New York society circles during the 1920s and 1930s.
Art of Leisure
April 12, 2025 – June 15, 2025
Elsie Whitmore Southwick Clark’s portrait of Jane Peterson catches the globetrotting artist in a rare moment of stillness. Dressed in walking clothes and carrying her portable supplies box, Peterson is depicted as a world traveler ready to explore and paint new lands.
For Peterson, traveling throughout Europe and the Mediterranean was an essential part of her artistic practice. She received acclaim for her interdisciplinary aesthetic that incorporated artistic styles like Fauvism and Impressionism that she learned while traveling abroad. With bold colors, visible brush strokes, and dynamic compositions, Peterson’s expressive paintings of Europe (left) show her attention to the cultural landscapes and artistic techniques of different regions.

artworks.title: Dancer, Harlem
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
For more than 80 years, James VanDerZee made photographs, capturing his family in their home of Lenox, Massachusetts; portraits marking significant moments; and scenes of everyday life in Harlem, New York. Working out of a commercial photography studio in the mostly Black neighborhood, including at the height of the Harlem Renaissance in the 1920s and 1930s, he photographed both ordinary people and leading Black artists and historical figures, becoming one of the most significant American photographers of the 20th century. He supplied elaborate backdrops and props in his studio and regularly retouched his negatives, often creating a soft focus, improving his sitters’ complexions, and sometimes even drawing jewelry on to wrists and necks in ways that are difficult, if not impossible, to discern in the finished prints.
VanDerZee has said: “Sometimes [the photographs] seemed to be more valuable to me than they did to the people I was photographing, because I put my heart and soul into them and tried to see that every picture was better looking than the person.”

artworks.title: Things Are Looking Native, Native's Looking Whiter
artworks.description:
Included in the exhibition:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
In this dual-portrait, Nicholas Galanin juxtaposes a photograph of a Hopi-Tewa woman, taken by Edward Curtis in 1906, with a promotional image of Carrie Fisher as Princess Leia in Star Wars, forcing viewers to confront stereotypes and societal biases.
Curtis took more than 40,000 photographs of Indigenous people in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, often posing his subjects in stereotypical ways and demeaning them as a “vanishing race.” Galanin, who is Tlingit and Unangax, has countered: “I’m still here and I’m still doing work. [Curtis] perpetuated these false ideas of purity and mystery.”
The two women have remarkably similar facial features and hairstyles, but whereas Fisher, at the time considered an ideal beauty, wore her hair as a costume to make her look alien and “other,” the unnamed woman’s squash blossom hairstyle is authentic to her culture. Galanin wants us to remember US history when considering this pairing: “The title speaks to consumer culture’s desire to claim ‘Native inspired’ looks while simultaneously refusing Indigenous people the agency to define Indigenous culture in an increasingly hybrid world.”

artworks.title: Self-Portrait
artworks.artist: Marisol Escobar (MARISOL), Universal Limited Art Editions
artworks.medium: intaglio on handmade Chatham British paper, handmade Chatham British paper, ink
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
Born to Venezuelan parents, Marisol grew up in Paris and Caracas before moving to the United States at age fifteen, where she earned acclaim and popularity. Primarily a sculptor and assemblage artist, her works are inspired by Pop art, pre-Columbian art, and folk art, as well as the contemporary artists on the New York scene, including Robert Rauschenberg, whose work is also displayed in this gallery. Although she often included elements of her own face or body in her work, she developed a persona as an elusive figure.
Self-Portrait is from the second body of work Marisol made with publisher and printer Universal Limited Art Editions (ULAE). There, she made multiple prints that incorporated tracings of her hands and feet interspersed with depictions of other objects; this print in particular was likely inspired by forms she saw in recent travels throughout Asia, Micronesia, and Polynesia.

artworks.title: I Have Returned
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
Since the mid-1960s, political cartoonist Patrick Oliphant’s cartoons have been published by newspapers across the United States through syndication. He brings his outrage toward political leaders into his work with “savagery,” as he’s described it, and 37th President Richard Nixon (1913–1994) became a subject.
Nixon famously became the only president to resign from office following confirmation of his involvement in a 1972 break-in of the Watergate office-apartment-hotel complex in Washington, DC, and its subsequent cover-up attempt. This image, made more than a decade later, deploys Nixon’s signature “V sign” pose—representing both victory and peace—and emphasizes a glare that suggests neither.

artworks.title: Portrait of Martha Pike
artworks.medium: Oil, oil on canvas, canvas, painting
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
William Jennys, an itinerant portrait painter, was trained in the craft by his father, Richard Jennys (c. 1734–c. 1809); the family immigrated from England to colonial America when William was a child.
At the time Jennys painted this portrait of a young Martha Pike (1801–1840s), probably in Newburyport, Massachusetts, father and son had been traveling throughout New England for about a decade making oil portraits. It is common in their portraits that the sitter, staged in a three-quarter view, looks directly out toward the viewer and sometimes hold a prop with one hand in front of their chest, as Pike does with her doll—perhaps a favorite toy or symbol of her young age.
Pike was four or five years old when this portrait was painted, preceding a difficult time in her family. Her father, Richard Pike, who married Sarah Boardman in 1800, worked as a merchant; Martha was the first born, followed by two more daughters: Sarah Jane, born in 1803 (and who lived until her early 60s), and Mary, born in 1805, and who died just over a year later. Sarah, the mother, passed in 1808. Richard and the two remaining children continued to live in Newburyport, where he likely had family support.
Nearly three decades later, in 1832, Martha married Roger Strong Howard (1807–1880) and had at least one child, a daughter, named after her mother and sister, Sarah Boardman Howard (1834–1889).

artworks.title: Julia Haring White
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
Julia Phelps Haring White (1850–1928) was born into a wealthy New York family. In 1874, after navigating two marriage proposals from two separate Georges, she wed George White, whose ancestors had settled Hartford in the 1630s. After marrying in Fairfield, the couple lived in Waterbury and had three children together. White’s time was interspersed with travel; she had even been in Europe for a period in the year this portrait was made, though she apparently always stayed up-to-date on Waterbury social news.
Painter Jeanette Harrison Shepperd Loop was born into a distinguished Connecticut family, affording her opportunities to pursue an artistic career. She studied under German émigré Louis Bail at the Yale School of Fine Arts before moving to New York City where she worked in the studio of Henry A. Loop, whom she would marry in 1864. She was elected an associate of the National Academy of Design in 1875—a recognition of excellence by her peers—and regularly exhibited with that organization. (A woman would not be elected as full member for more than four decades.)
White and Loop, who also painted George White’s portrait at this time, may have learned of each other through their Connecticut social circles.

artworks.title: Connecticut Tobacco Nets
artworks.description:
Included in the exhibition:
Staff Favorites from the Mattatuck Collection, January 18, 2026 – April 12, 2026
“One of the most rewarding aspects of engaging with art is discovering a connection that makes a piece feel more accessible and personal. This image transports the viewer to the unique landscape of Connecticut’s agricultural history, capturing the canopies that once stretched across the tobacco fields. These nets protected the fragile, broadleaf plants that were prized for cigar wrappers and brought a distinctive look.
For me, this photograph brings to mind a story about my mother. She grew up in Windsor Locks near the tobacco fields. As a young girl, she was excited by the prospect of spending a summer working in those very fields, a rite of passage for many of her peers. However, her dream was quickly dashed when my grandfather let her know that she would not be working a summer in the tobacco fields. This piece becomes a vessel for shared family history and memory. I would be remiss not to mention that despite there being significantly less tobacco fields than in the past, there are still around 44 farms, covering 3,056 acres producing shade tobacco in Connecticut.” - Staff Member: Jason Foberg
Director of Education

artworks.title: Elkanah Doolittle
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
(Referring to this artwork as well as James Herring, Hannah Compton Doolittle, c. 1815–1825, 84.30.2) A Connecticut-born graduate of Yale College (1789, possibly graduating as a Doctor of Sacred Theology), Elkanah Doolittle (1767–1835) taught at the Sunbury Academy in Georgia for some years before ultimately settling in New York City, where he worked as a manufacturer of soaps, candles, glues, and other material made from tallow (animal fat). His first wife, Abigail, with whom he shared two children, died in 1801 at the age of 26. It is unknown when exactly he met his second wife, Hannah Compton (1780–1830), but they married on November 5, 1803, in Brooklyn and had five children.
In the 1810s or 1820s, the couple’s portraits were painted by James Herring—a staunch promoter of the arts who edited the influential book The National Portrait Gallery of Distinguished Americans, which laid the foundation for what would open in 1968 as the National Portrait Gallery in Washington, DC. Around the time of their portrait sittings, Elkanah was a trustee for the First Presbyterian Church of Brooklyn and involved in Brooklyn’s first bank. As is common in the historical records for women at this time, very little is known about Hannah. One might wonder how she managed a house of 9—herself and Elkanah and seven children, all listed together in the 1830 census.

artworks.title: View of Horace Johnson's Art Studio
artworks.description:
Horace Chauncey Johnson (1820-1890) was the preëminent Waterbury portrait painter of his day and stood at the center of Waterbury's art world. This photograph depicts his art studio with his paintings hanging on the wall, leaning on the floor, and one ready to be worked on in an easel. A small table to the right of the easel has a palette and quite a few bottles on top of it.

artworks.title: Portrait of Minnie Rogers Steele
artworks.description:
This photograph depicts Waterbury artist Minnie Rogers Steele. On the reverse Joel Anderson wrote a brief biography "Minnie Rogers Steele 1860-1940. Waterbury Artist; studied with William Cummings Chase, Charles Webster Hawthorne, and Charles Neville Dewey at the Art Students League in New York. In the 1920's, her interest in art took her to Japan. Some of her paintings show the influence of this trip. In later life dissatisfaction with the stereotypical painting of the times took her to Paris where she studied with Andre Lhote, a modernist, influencing her finest work.

artworks.title: James Mitchell Lamson Scovill
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
Waterbury-born James Mitchell Lamson Scovill (1789–1857) co-founded his first company in 1811 and went on to create the firm that would become Scovill Manufacturing Company in 1850. The company manufactured gilt buttons, daguerreotype plates and other photographic equipment, and additional metal goods.
As a prominent businessman, Scovill had multiple portraits made during and after his lifetime. This silhouette represents a popular 19th-century format that was affordable to more people, especially before photographic technology spread widely. But Scovill’s portrait is no ordinary silhouette—it is made by leading artist Auguste Edouart, who cut depictions of people throughout England, Scotland, the United States, and his home country of France, making thousands of images in his lifetime.

artworks.title: Self-Portrait
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
Charles Akers likely painted this self-portrait while he was still living in his home state of Maine; he moved away sometime after Portland’s Great Fire of 1866 and traveled to Boston, New York, and Connecticut. Notably, he did not establish an art career as a painter, but rather, as a sculptor, crayon artist, and writer (perhaps taking after his older brother, Benjamin Paul [1825–1861]).
In H.W. French’s 1879 book Art and Artists in Connecticut, Charles Akers is described as “the sculptor and crayon artist, at present established in New York, in 1860, 1869, and 1875 occupied a studio in Waterbury, Conn., making crayon heads and marble busts which were both artistic and popular. He is an artist of much merit, and an elegant writer.” Despite this praise received during his lifetime, little is known of Akers today.

artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
A self-taught portrait painter, Ralph Earl spent his early career in New Haven and learned his craft through the careful observation and emulation of esteemed painters, including John Singleton Copley. During the Revolutionary War, he sided with the loyalists, and in 1778, he moved to England and studied with artist Benjamin West. Returning in 1785, after the war’s end, he painted in Boston, Providence, and New York City.

artworks.title: Mark Twain
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
Samuel Clemens (1835–1910), best known by his pen name Mark Twain, is often referred to as the “father of American literature.” His early years were shaped by his family’s life on the banks of the Mississippi River in Missouri, which was then part of the country’s western border. When he was 11 years old, his father died, and he worked various jobs around the country, including as a printer’s apprentice, a steamboat pilot, and a news reporter before achieving a career as a writer.
Throughout his life, his views evolved: he was born into a Southern family who enslaved African Americans, but he later became an outspoken critic of racism, imperialism, and religious hypocrisy. In his books, he often critiqued the rapid industrialization, massive immigration, and social inequality of the period.
Connecticut shaped the most productive chapter of Twain’s life: he moved to Hartford in 1871 with his wife, Olivia Langdon Clemens, to be closer to his publisher and there the couple raised three daughters; he resided in the state for nearly two decades. In Hartford, he wrote many of his important novels, including Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, The Prince and the Pauper, and A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court. His legacy is maintained through his home: the Mark Twain House and Museum stands as a National Historic Landmark in Hartford, preserving the same space where an American voice thrived.

artworks.title: Checkers Up At The Farm
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
At a time when professional art was out of reach for many middle-class families, John Rogers developed plaster-cast sculptures that could be produced in high editions and sold at relatively affordable prices. He sold around 80,000 of these sculptures, featuring around 80 designs, typically genre scenes—portraits of families at home or other scenes of American life.
We invite you to use this sculpture to practice drawing people of all ages. Drawing from sculpture is a way to learn more about the three-dimensionality of the human form and expressions in lieu of live models. As a student in c. 1920, artist Kay Sage, whose works are on view in this gallery, practiced drawing heads, hands, and figures from sculptures, among learning other foundational techniques; years later, she expanded her skills and became a prominent surrealist.

artworks.description:
Included in the exhibition:
Staff Favorites from the Mattatuck Collection, January 18, 2026 – April 12, 2026
“As part of an ongoing project for the Museum Shop, I’ve been developing a line of merchandise inspired by vintage logos, marketing pieces, and branded packaging found in the Museum’s collection. This work has led me deep into our collections storage spaces—places filled with hidden gems and local history that often go unseen by the public.
While exploring, I discovered a wide range of objects that reflect the entrepreneurial spirit and design sensibilities of Waterbury and the surrounding region over the past century. From quirky packaging to beautifully designed labels, these items tell the story of businesses that once thrived here and the unique ways they presented their products to the world.
This project has reminded me how much character and creativity can be found in everyday objects. My staff pick is a few of the many pieces that caught my eye—not just for their visual appeal, but for the history and sense of place they represent. Maybe they will even spark a memory for you. I hope they give you a glimpse into the rich commercial and design heritage of our area.” - Staff Member: Stephanie Harris
Deputy Director
